messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 43

# Michael's Case

Michael sits in the office with the careful posture of someone who has learned to take up as little space as possible. At fifty-eight, he carries himself with the precision that has defined his career as a forensic analyst—shoulders squared, hands steady, eyes that notice everything. But there is a brittleness to him now, a sense that he might fracture if someone looked too closely.

Seven years ago, Michael was working at the industrial chemical plant where he had spent thirty-two years. He had built his reputation analyzing contamination patterns, tracing sources of chemical leaks, writing reports that other analysts cited in their own work. He took pride in this. His wife, Rosa, used to joke that he could find a needle in a haystack—he just needed the right microscope.

The explosion happened on a Tuesday morning in March. Michael was in the lab when the storage tank in Unit Seven ruptured. He remembers the sound first—not loud exactly, but wrong, a percussion that seemed to come from inside his own chest. Then the building moved. He was thrown against the steel counter, his left shoulder taking the impact. Around him, glass containers shattered. Someone screamed. The emergency lights came on, bathing everything in red.

Forty-three people died. Twelve were never fully identified.

Michael survived with a fractured clavicle and lacerations on his face and hands. The physical injuries healed within months. Everything else has been slower.

For the first year after, Michael returned to work. He had to. The company brought in investigators, and his expertise was needed to understand what had failed. He found himself walking through the wreckage, photographing the twisted metal, collecting samples from the contamination zone. His hands did the work automatically. His mind was somewhere else—still in that moment when the world rearranged itself.

Now, seven years later, Michael has taken a leave of absence. He tells Rosa he is thinking about retirement, but the truth is more complicated. He cannot be in enclosed spaces without his chest tightening. The lab where he spent three decades feels like a tomb. He has nightmares three or four nights a week—not always about the explosion itself, but about standing in the ruins afterward, realizing that the precision and control he had cultivated meant nothing. That a system could fail catastrophically despite all the safeguards, all the protocols, all the careful analysis.

He startles at loud noises. Rosa has learned to warn him before she uses the blender. He finds himself checking the structural integrity of their house obsessively, running his hands along walls, looking for cracks. His mind generates scenarios constantly—what if the foundation shifts, what if the roof collapses, what if the gas line ruptures. He knows these thoughts are irrational. He knows this because he is intelligent and educated and has spent his career understanding systems and failure modes. Knowing does not help.

He has stopped seeing his friends. He has stopped going to his daughter's soccer games. Work, the thing that defined him for thirty-two years, now feels impossible. He sits at home most days, reading news articles about industrial disasters, studying photographs of damaged plants, as though understanding the mechanics of failure might somehow prevent the next catastrophe.

Rosa watches him with worried eyes. She asks gentle questions. Michael answers with half-truths because he does not know how to explain that the world feels fundamentally unstable now, that his expertise has become a liability, that he cannot stop imagining all the ways things can break.
